The key consequence is that there is no post-deployment learning loop, so the real-garden gap has to be closed before release; I rewrote the training story to bake in phone-photo robustness with photorealistic augmentation, and added a lightweight on-device sanity check that gates the top-three output and feeds the unsure fallback. idea.title: Leaf-photo plant disease check for home gardeners
idea.one_liner: Let a gardener photograph a sick leaf with their phone and get told which disease it probably is.
idea.description: A phone app that runs entirely on the device — no server and no network connection needed — where the gardener photographs a leaf that looks wrong. An image classifier, fine-tuned on labelled photographs of diseased leaves and quantized to run on the phone, returns the three most likely diseases with a confidence for each, plus a short description of what to do about the top one. Because the app never uploads photos, it cannot learn from real usage after release; instead the model is trained before release with photorealistic augmentation (cluttered backgrounds, lighting and white-balance shifts, motion blur, rotation, perspective) so it is robust to the photos gardeners actually take. The claim is that most common garden diseases are visually distinctive enough that a phone photo is sufficient, so no lab test or expert is needed for the everyday cases.
idea.problem: Home gardeners cannot tell plant diseases apart, so they either do nothing or spray the wrong treatment.

sections.technique: Fine-tune an off-the-shelf image classifier on a public dataset of labelled diseased-leaf photographs, then quantize and compress it so inference runs entirely on the phone. The photo never leaves the device and the app works offline. The trade-off of dropping the server is that there is no post-deployment learning loop — user photos can never be collected for later model improvement — so the real-garden gap must be closed before release: train with photorealistic augmentation (random cluttered backgrounds, lighting and white-balance shifts, motion blur, leaf rotation and perspective). The app runs a lightweight on-device sanity check before classification (is this a leaf, and is the damage disease-like?) that gates the top-three output and feeds the 'unsure about all three' fallback. Show the top three, not just the best guess, so the gardener can tell when the model is unsure.
open_questions: Does photorealistic augmentation during training make the shipped on-device model robust enough to real garden photos, given there is no post-deployment learning loop?
When the sanity check fails or all three confidences are low, what exactly should the app say and do for the gardener?

nodes.text:
# Leaf-photo plant disease check for home gardeners
_Let a gardener photograph a sick leaf with their phone and get told which disease it probably is._

## the problem it addresses
Home gardeners cannot tell plant diseases apart, so they either do nothing or spray the wrong treatment.

## description
A phone app where the gardener photographs a leaf that looks wrong. An image classifier trained on labelled photographs of diseased leaves returns the three most likely diseases with a confidence for each, plus a short description of what to do about the top one. The claim is that most common garden diseases are visually distinctive enough that a phone photo is sufficient, so no lab test or expert is needed for the everyday cases.

## addresses gaps
gap_demo01

## technique
Fine-tune an off-the-shelf image classifier on a public dataset of labelled diseased-leaf photographs. The app sends the photo to a server, the server returns the top three labels with confidences. Show the top three, not just the best guess, so the gardener can tell when the model is unsure.

## open_questions
- Do photos taken in a real garden work as well as the clean dataset photos taken against a plain background?
- How should the app behave when the model is unsure about all three guesses?
nodes.title: Leaf-photo plant disease check for home gardeners

nodes.text: Swap the fine-tune target from a server-grade classifier to a mobile-optimized one (e.g. MobileNet or EfficientNet-Lite) distilled from the original, quantized to int8/fp16, and converted to CoreML/TFLite so inference runs fully offline. The disease descriptions and treatment texts become a static JSON asset shipped in the app bundle, so nothing about the answer pipeline needs a network. The uncertainty behavior stays 'show the top three with confidences', but since the model is frozen at install time, the honest fallback when all confidences are low is local: general leaf-health advice plus a pointer to a local extension service — no server round-trip. This is the minimal faithful rewrite: same mechanism, moved wholesale onto the phone.
nodes.title: Rewrite around a bundled, quantized mobile model with a local knowledge base; the app-store release is the only update path.
nodes.comparison: Faithful, concrete rewrite of the same mechanism onto the phone (quantized MobileNet/EfficientNet-Lite, local JSON knowledge base, local fallback), but it restates the no-server requirement with standard tooling and leaves the real-garden-photo open question unresolved.

nodes.text: Because the phone can never upload photos for later model improvement, the real-garden gap must be closed before release: train the mobile classifier with photorealistic augmentation — random cluttered backgrounds, lighting and white-balance shifts, motion blur, leaf rotation and perspective — so the shipped model is robust to the photos gardeners actually take. The app itself gains a lightweight on-device sanity check before classification (is this a leaf, and is the damage disease-like?) that gates the top-three output and feeds the 'unsure about all three' fallback. This keeps the single image-classifier mechanism but makes the training set, not a server, carry the responsibility for real-world accuracy.

nodes.question: Does photorealistic augmentation close the phone-photo accuracy gap for the mobile classifier within, say, 5 percentage points of clean-dataset accuracy?
